blocks.h2: Does Your Sewer Line Need Repair?
blocks.intro: A sewer line problem doesn't always mean a full replacement. Most issues start smaller than that, and catching them early is what keeps them that way. Here's how to know where you stand:

tiles.h3: Slow Drains or Gurgling That Keep Coming Back After Rodding
tiles.body: If rodding clears it but the same slow drain or gurgling returns within a few months, the clog isn't the real problem. Something further down the line is catching debris again.

tiles.h3: Recurring Backups or Pooling Water in the Yard
tiles.body: A backup that keeps happening, or a soggy patch in the yard, points to something wrong with the pipe itself, not a one-time clog. Rodding alone probably won't hold this time.

tiles.h3: Confirmed Crack, Joint Separation, or Root Intrusion on Camera
tiles.body: Once a camera inspection confirms damage to the pipe, this isn't a rodding job anymore. We'll walk you through what repair looks like for your line.

blocks.h2: Why Sewer Lines Fail in Highland Park
blocks.intro: The median home in Highland Park was built in 1963, and about 1 in 4 went up before 1940. Add wooded ravines and mature trees, and you get the three causes we'd check first on any Highland Park sewer line.

items.h3: Clay and Cast Iron That Have Reached Their Age
items.body: Homes built before the 1970s often have clay or cast iron sewer lines. Clay typically lasts 50 to 60 years and is especially vulnerable to cracking at the joints. Cast iron usually lasts 50 to 75 years, but corrodes from the inside as it ages. Nearly half of Highland Park homes were built before 1960, so many lines here are at or past that range.

items.h3: Roots From Ravines and Tree-Lined Streets
items.body: Roots grow toward any source of moisture, and a sewer line is exactly that. Once a root finds a crack or a loose joint, it keeps growing until it blocks the flow or cracks the pipe further. If roots are the only problem, [hydro jetting](/highland-park/hydro-jetting) can clear them. If they've already broken the pipe, it's a repair.

Lake County winters mean years of ground freezing and thawing around your pipe. Joints take the strain and can separate, or the pipe can settle into a low spot, called a belly, where waste collects instead of flowing through.

items.h3: The Line Is Yours to Fix
items.body: In Highland Park, the homeowner owns and maintains the private sewer line from the house to the city main. When that line cracks or collapses, the repair is on you, not the city. That's why we show you the footage and the exact location of the damage before recommending anything.

blocks.h2: How We Repair a Sewer Line
blocks.intro: Once we know what's wrong, there's usually more than one way to fix it. Which method makes sense depends on the pipe's condition, location, and how it failed.
head: Method
What It Involves
Typical Disruption
rows: A resin-coated liner is pulled through the existing pipe and cured in place, creating a new pipe inside the old one.
Minimal digging, usually just small access points
A new pipe is pulled through the old one while a bursting head fractures the old pipe outward to make room.
Minimal digging, works even when the old pipe is badly damaged
The damaged section is dug up and replaced directly.
More digging, but sometimes the only option depending on damage location and access
blocks.note: On wooded Highland Park lots, a method that saves mature trees and landscaping is often worth asking about. Your technician will walk you through which method fits your situation after the camera inspection.

blocks.h2: Sewer Repair Questions From Highland Park Homeowners

items.q: Who pays to fix a sewer line in Highland Park, the city or the homeowner?
items.preview: The homeowner. You own the private sewer line from your house to the city main.
items.answer: In Highland Park, the homeowner owns and maintains the private sewer line that runs from the house to the city main. If that line cracks, separates or fills with roots, the repair is yours to handle. A [camera inspection](/highland-park/video-camera-sewer-inspections) shows exactly where the problem is before you commit to anything.

items.q: Can a sewer line be repaired without digging up my yard?
items.preview: Often, yes. Trenchless methods work through small access points. The camera shows if your line qualifies.
items.answer: Often, yes. Trenchless lining and pipe bursting fix the line through one or two small access points, which matters on Highland Park lots with mature trees, ravine slopes and established landscaping. A fully collapsed section or a severe belly may still need a spot dig. The camera tells us which applies to your line. See [trenchless sewer repair](/highland-park/trenchless-sewer-repair).

items.q: Is my older clay sewer line going to fail?
items.preview: Not necessarily. Clay lasts 50 to 60 years, so a camera check tells you where yours stands.
items.answer: Not necessarily, but it's worth checking. About 1 in 4 Highland Park homes was built before 1940, and clay typically lasts 50 to 60 years before the joints start to crack and let roots in. Age alone doesn't mean something is wrong. A camera inspection shows the real condition so you can plan a repair instead of reacting to a backup.

items.q: How much does sewer line repair cost in Highland Park?
items.preview: It depends on the damage, the depth and the repair method. You get a flat price before work begins.
items.answer: It depends on what the camera finds: the type of damage, how deep and long the affected section is, the repair method, and what's above the line, like a driveway, patio or mature trees. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins, so you know the cost going in. Give us a call and we'll walk you through it.

items.q: Should I repair or replace my sewer line?
items.preview: A single damaged section usually means repair. Damage along most of the line usually means replacement.
items.answer: If the damage is limited to one section and the rest of the pipe is sound, a repair usually makes sense. If the camera shows cracks, root intrusion and corrosion along most of the line, replacing it can save you from paying for repeat repairs. We'll tell you straight which one we'd pick for your line, and why.
